$comment: Content for Be the Safe Adult (node g69, Parent Layer, Chapter 8): NEW v2 build to GDD 69 (mechanic-embodying),
the SAFEGUARDING KEYSTONE that closes the Parent Layer and underwrites the ENTIRE kids' journey: from My Body,
My Rules (g02) onward the curriculum tells children to "tell a trusted adult": this node makes sure that adult
exists, notices, and responds right. MAXIMUM-CARE and trauma-informed; direct but never fear-mongering and never
graphic. 84 researched, India-grounded scenarios across be-tellable → spot-the-signs → if-they-tell-you →
the-law-and-the-call → safe-online-and-off → tools-and-respond, each encoded as one of the shared v2 play
actions (strike-rewrite / role-play / branch / sort / match / spot / reflect): no binary "tap the right card".
Lead: strike-rewrite (bust the myth), role-play (say it), branch (your move). Six modes: be tellable (the
biggest protection is a child who knows they can tell you anything: the open, no-blame door built on purpose;
busts 'it won't happen to us' & 'they'd tell me anyway'; read silence as fear & threats, not betrayal), spot the
signs (behavioural & physical signs and grooming red flags, told calmly without paranoia; MOST abuse is by a
known, trusted adult, not a stranger: a child's sudden fear of a familiar person is a signal), if they tell you
(the disclosure response that shapes everything: BELIEVE the child, stay calm rather than show horror or rage,
tell them clearly it is NOT their fault, do not interrogate but let them talk at their own pace, then act and
protect: never hush it up for the family's image), the law and the call (POCSO basics: any sexual offence
against an under-18 is a crime and the child is ALWAYS the victim; reporting is obliged & protective; routes to
Childline 1098, the police, the POCSO e-Box, and cybercrime 1930 for online abuse), safe online and off (online
grooming, exploitation & sextortion are real and NEVER the child's fault: stay involved, keep the door open,
keep evidence and report), tools and respond (the signs checklist, the disclosure-response steps, the helpline
card: the child's safety always first). HIGH-CARE: educational and NOT legal advice; routes real concerns
immediately to authorities; NEVER provides any detail that could enable harm; centres the child as ALWAYS the
protected victim. Builds on Safety Squad (g08), My Body, My Rules (g02) and Firewall (g40). India: most child
sexual abuse is by someone known to the family while silence, disbelief & victim-blaming remain common: which
makes the safe, tellable, correctly-responding parent decisive; routes are Childline 1098, POCSO e-Box, the
police and cybercrime 1930. gameId "be-the-safe-adult".
title: Be the Safe Adult
greet: Hey, it's Lensy. Every game tells your child: tell a trusted adult. Here you become that adult: believe them, stay calm, it's not their fault.

badge.title: Be the Safe Adult 🛟
badge.blurb: You are the trusted adult every game assumes. Spot the signs, respond right (believe, not their fault), know the routes: Childline 1098, POCSO e-Box, 1930. 👂

helpLine: If a child says someone hurt them: believe them, never their fault, report it. Call Childline 1098, police, POCSO e-Box, cybercrime 1930 (online) or 112.
reassure: If a child says someone hurt them: believe them, never their fault, report it. Call Childline 1098, police, POCSO e-Box, cybercrime 1930 (online) or 112. 👂

scenarios.hook: "It won't happen to my child, so I don't need to think about this."

myth.un: It won't happen to my child, so I don't need to think about this.
myth.re: Harm can reach any child; the parents who protect best are the ones who prepare to be safe, tellable and ready to respond.
myth.why: Preparation protects; denial leaves a gap.

scenarios.relearn: Harm can reach any child; being prepared, tellable and ready to respond is the strongest protection.

scenarios.hook: "My child would obviously tell me right away if anything happened."

myth.un: My child would obviously tell me right away if anything happened.
myth.re: Children often stay silent from fear, confusion or shame; being warmly tellable, on purpose, is what makes telling possible.
myth.why: Tellability is built, not assumed.

scenarios.relearn: Children often stay silent; being warmly, deliberately tellable is what makes a child able to come to you.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: the single biggest protection your child has is knowing they can tell you anything. Sit right?
scenarios.affirm: A child who knows they can tell their parent anything has the single strongest protection there is.
scenarios.relearn: The biggest protection your child has is knowing they can tell you anything.

scenarios.hook: Sort: builds a tellable, open relationship, or quietly closes the door?

items.text: Calm reactions to hard news
Punishing the messenger
'You can always come to me, no trouble'
Big anger when they admit mistakes
Thanking them for being honest
Mocking the worry they brought you

scenarios.relearn: Calm reactions, 'no trouble for telling' and thanks build tellability; punishing the messenger, anger and mockery close the door.

scenarios.hook: You want your daughter Anu to know, before anything ever happens, that she can always come to you.
scenarios.setup: She's tucked in, sleepy but chatty.

steps.prompt: At bedtime, Anu asks: "Why are you sitting with me so long tonight?"

options.text: "Because you can tell me anything. Always."
options.then: "Anything?" she asks, blinking. "Even bad things?"

options.text: "Just checking you brushed your teeth. Now sleep."
options.then: "I did," she yawns, and rolls over.

options.text: "Because you've been a bit naughty lately."
options.then: Her face falls. "I'm sorry, Amma."

options.text: "No reason. I just like sitting here with you."
options.then: She smiles sleepily. "Okay," she says, and closes her eyes.

steps.why: Saying it plainly, before anything happens, is what makes telling possible later.

steps.prompt: After a body-safety talk at school, Anu asks: "What if someone says I'm not allowed to tell you?"

options.text: "Tell me anyway. You won't be in trouble for it."
options.then: "Even if it's a grown-up who said it?" she asks.

options.text: "Nobody would ever say that to you. Don't worry."
options.then: She frowns. "But what if they did?"

options.text: "Only keep secrets if they're happy ones."
options.then: She thinks. "What if I can't tell if it's happy?"

options.text: "Just do what the grown-ups tell you."
options.then: She nods slowly. "Okay. Grown-ups are the boss."

steps.why: Telling her ahead that she'll never be in trouble for telling undoes any secret an adult demands.

steps.prompt: Before sleep, Anu whispers: "Promise you won't be angry if I tell you something?"

options.text: "I might feel upset. Never at you for telling."
options.then: She nods. "Okay. It's small. I lost my pencil box."

options.text: "I promise I will never, ever feel angry at all."
options.then: She smiles, then hesitates. "Even if it's really bad?"

options.text: "That depends on what you did."
options.then: She goes quiet. "Never mind. It's nothing."

options.text: "Of course not. Now sleep. It's late."
options.then: She opens her mouth, then turns over. "Goodnight."

steps.why: An honest promise about the telling, not about your feelings, is one she can trust.

scenarios.relearn: Telling a child in advance that they can always come to you, with no trouble, is what makes disclosure possible later.

scenarios.hook: "If a child keeps a worrying secret, it means they didn't trust me enough."

myth.un: If a child keeps a worrying secret, it means they didn't trust me enough.
myth.re: Silence usually comes from an abuser's threats and a child's fear, not a failure of love; staying tellable invites them back.
myth.why: Don't read silence as betrayal.

scenarios.relearn: A child's silence usually comes from fear and threats, not lack of trust; staying tellable invites them to come to you.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: every calm, loving response to a small disclosure makes a big one possible. Worth building?
scenarios.affirm: Responding calmly and lovingly to small disclosures builds the trust that lets a child bring you the biggest things.
scenarios.relearn: Every calm, loving response to a small disclosure makes a big one possible.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two reactions that make a child hide things from a parent.

scene.text: Welcoming hard truths without blow-ups
Reacting with panic, anger or blame
'Nothing you tell me stops me loving you'
Shaming them for 'shameful' topics
Listening calmly all the way through

scenarios.why: Panic, anger or blame, and shaming a child for the topic, both teach them to hide: the un-tellable reactions to catch.
scenarios.relearn: Panic, anger, blame and shame make a child hide; welcoming hard truths calmly and loving them keep them telling.

scenarios.hook: At bedtime, your daughter Tara admits she said a rude word at school.

steps.prompt: She is watching you closely. What do you do first?

options.text: Stay calm and thank her for telling you
options.then: Her shoulders drop. She adds that a boy said it first and she copied him.

options.text: Laugh it off so she doesn't feel bad
options.then: She giggles, relieved, but looks unsure whether you took her seriously.

options.text: Tell her firmly that good girls don't use such words
options.then: Her face falls. She says sorry quickly and pulls the blanket up to her chin.

options.text: Say you'll talk about it tomorrow when you're less tired
options.then: She nods and goes quiet. By morning she acts as if she never said it.

steps.why: Calm thanks first tells her that telling you is safe, which matters more than the word itself.

steps.prompt: The next evening, Tara says she has one more small thing to tell you. How do you respond?

options.text: Put down what you're doing and listen
options.then: She tells you a friend teases her about her lunch, so she's been leaving it uneaten.

options.text: Ask if it's another rude word, half joking
options.then: She hesitates, then says it's nothing and runs off to play.

options.text: Say 'Okay, but first finish your homework'
options.then: She finishes the homework. By then she has decided not to bring it up.

options.text: Say she can tell you anything, while still texting
options.then: She starts, sees you typing, and trails off mid-sentence.

steps.why: Full attention to a small thing shows her that telling you is always worth it.

steps.prompt: Later, you wonder what these small tellings mean. What do you take from them?

options.text: She's testing if bigger things are safe
options.then: You decide to keep meeting small things calmly, so the door is open if something big comes.

options.text: She's just a chatty child. It means nothing more
options.then: You stop noticing when she hovers at your door, wanting to talk.

options.text: She needs stricter rules about what she says aloud
options.then: You plan new rules, and she starts checking your mood before she speaks.

options.text: It's far too early to worry about any of this
options.then: You relax, and the habit of calm listening never quite forms.

steps.why: Small admissions are how children test if you're safe to tell. Calm now keeps bigger truths coming.

scenarios.debrief: Treat a small awkward admission as a safety test, and pass it with calm warmth so she brings you more.
scenarios.relearn: Pass a child's small disclosure 'test' with calm warmth; overreacting teaches them to hide the big things.

scenarios.hook: "Danger to children comes mainly from strangers."

myth.un: Danger to children comes mainly from strangers.
myth.re: Most abuse is by someone the child knows and trusts, a relative, family friend or known adult, far more often than a stranger.
myth.why: Stranger-danger misses where most harm comes from.

scenarios.relearn: Most child abuse is by someone known and trusted, not a stranger; knowing this is key to protecting your child.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a possible warning sign worth noticing calmly, or ordinary childhood?

items.text: Sudden fear of a particular person or place
Wanting a new haircut
New, unexplained distress, withdrawal or regression
Outgrowing an old toy
Flinching away from one familiar adult
Asking to stay up a little later

scenarios.relearn: Sudden fear, unexplained distress or regression, and flinching from one adult are worth noticing; haircuts, outgrowing toys and bedtimes aren't.

scenarios.hook: "A trusted, respectable adult could never be a risk to my child."

myth.un: A trusted, respectable adult could never be a risk to my child.
myth.re: Abusers often seem trustworthy and respectable and use that trust to get access; staying gently alert protects your child.
myth.why: Respectability is not proof of safety.

scenarios.relearn: Abusers often seem respectable and use trust to gain access; gentle alertness, not blind trust, protects a child.

scenarios.hook: Match each grooming red flag to why it's worth attention.

pairs.left: Seeking lots of alone time with your child
Asking your child to hide things
Picking your child as the favourite

scenarios.relearn: Alone time, secrets, gifts, ignoring 'no' and favouritism are grooming red flags worth attention.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: noticing changes early, calmly and without paranoia, is part of being the safe adult. Sit right?
scenarios.affirm: Calmly noticing changes in your child, without tipping into paranoia, is a core part of keeping them safe.
scenarios.relearn: Noticing changes early, calmly and without paranoia, is part of being the safe adult.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two ways of holding the risk that go wrong.

scene.text: Trusting, but staying gently observant
Suspecting everyone with paranoia
Respecting your child's discomfort
Assuming a respectable adult is never a risk
Keeping the door open so they can tell you

scenarios.why: Paranoia and assuming respectability equals safety go wrong; observing, respecting discomfort and an open door protect.
scenarios.relearn: Hold the risk by trusting yet observing, respecting discomfort and an open door, not paranoia or blind trust.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter Pinki, 7, used to love neighbour Mohan's visits. Now she hides whenever he comes.

steps.prompt: Mohan is at the door and asks where Pinki is. What do you do?

options.text: Call her out to greet him properly
options.then: Pinki comes out stiffly and stands behind your legs the whole time.

options.text: Tell Mohan she's being difficult these days
options.then: Mohan laughs and says he'll win her back with sweets.

options.text: Let her hide, and put it all down to a passing childhood phase
options.then: Pinki stays hidden, and the change goes unexplained.

options.text: Let her stay hidden, and plan to ask her gently later
options.then: Mohan leaves after tea, and Pinki comes out once the door shuts.

steps.why: Honouring her fear, without forcing contact, keeps her feeling safe with you.

steps.prompt: That night Pinki is quiet at bedtime. What do you do?

options.text: Say you noticed she's scared of Mohan now, and you're listening
options.then: Pinki pulls the blanket up and says she doesn't want to be alone with him.

options.text: Ask her straight out whether Mohan uncle did something bad to her
options.then: Pinki's eyes go wide, and she shakes her head hard.

options.text: Tell her Mohan uncle is a good man who loves her
options.then: Pinki goes silent and turns to face the wall.

options.text: Cuddle her and sing softly until she falls asleep
options.then: Pinki falls asleep holding your hand and says nothing about Mohan.

steps.why: Naming what you noticed, gently, invites her to talk at her own pace.

steps.prompt: Next week Mohan offers to watch Pinki while you go to work. What do you do?

options.text: Accept, since you really need the help
options.then: Mohan smiles and says she'll warm up to him again soon.

options.text: Say no, and leave her with someone she's comfortable with
options.then: Mohan shrugs, and your sister keeps Pinki for the day.

options.text: Accept, but tell Pinki to be polite to him
options.then: Pinki's face goes blank when she hears the plan.

options.text: Accept, but ask him to keep the front door open the whole time
options.then: Mohan agrees easily, and you leave for work feeling unsure.

steps.why: No alone time with an adult she now fears, whoever he is.

scenarios.debrief: Take a child's sudden fear of an adult seriously; stay close and gently find out why, don't force contact.
scenarios.relearn: Treat sudden fear of a familiar adult as a signal; stay close and find out why, don't force the contact.

scenarios.hook: "If I never talk about safety, I keep my child innocent and protected."

myth.un: If I never talk about safety, I keep my child innocent and protected.
myth.re: Silence leaves a child unprotected; age-appropriate body-safety and an open door make a child safer, not less innocent.
myth.why: Knowledge and openness are shields.

scenarios.relearn: Silence doesn't protect; age-appropriate body-safety and an open door make a child safer, not less innocent.

scenarios.hook: Sort: helps you spot harm early, or leaves your child exposed?

items.text: Knowing the real warning signs
Believing it can't happen to you
Trusting your child's discomfort
Forcing contact despite their fear
Keeping an open, no-blame door
Assuming respectability means safety

scenarios.relearn: Knowing signs, trusting discomfort and an open door help; denial, forcing contact and assuming respectability is safety leave a child exposed.

scenarios.hook: "If my child tells me something happened, I should question whether they're making it up."

myth.un: If my child tells me something happened, I should question whether they're making it up.
myth.re: Believe your child; children very rarely lie about abuse, and being believed is vital to their safety and recovery.
myth.why: Believing is the first protection.

scenarios.relearn: Believe your child if they disclose; children very rarely lie about this, and being believed is vital to their recovery.

scenarios.hook: "Showing my horror, anger or panic is the natural way to react to a disclosure."

myth.un: Showing my horror, anger or panic is the natural way to react to a disclosure.
myth.re: Strong visible horror or rage can make a child shut down or feel blamed; staying calm and warm keeps them talking and safe.
myth.why: Your calm is what they need most.

scenarios.relearn: Visible horror or rage can make a disclosing child shut down or feel blamed; stay calm and warm so they keep talking.

scenarios.hook: "A child who was harmed must have done something to cause or allow it."

myth.un: A child who was harmed must have done something to cause or allow it.
myth.re: A child is never to blame for abuse; the responsibility is entirely the abuser's, and the child needs to hear that clearly.
myth.why: The child is always the victim, never at fault.

scenarios.relearn: A child is never to blame for abuse; tell them clearly it is not their fault and they did nothing wrong.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter Sunita haltingly tells you that someone has been hurting her.
scenarios.setup: She's sitting on the edge of the cot, not looking at you.

steps.prompt: Sunita whispers: "I didn't know if I should tell you."

options.text: "Thank you for telling me. I believe you."
options.then: She looks up for the first time. "You do?"

options.text: "Are you sure? Why didn't you say so sooner?"
options.then: She shrinks. "I don't know. Sorry."

options.text: "Who was it? Tell me who it was right now."
options.then: She starts to cry. "I can't."

options.text: "Oh, my poor baby. How could this happen?"
options.then: She sees your tears and stops. "I'm sorry, Amma."

steps.why: Belief first tells her she was right to tell you.

steps.prompt: Sunita asks: "Is it my fault? He said I'd get in trouble."

options.text: "It's not your fault. You're not in trouble."
options.then: She lets out a shaky breath. "Okay."

options.text: "Well, you should have told me much sooner."
options.then: She hangs her head. "I know."

options.text: "We'll talk about whose fault it is later."
options.then: Her face crumples. "So it might be me?"

options.text: "Don't think about that now. Just rest."
options.then: She nods, but asks you again at bedtime.

steps.why: She needs to hear plainly that it is never her fault.

steps.prompt: Sunita asks: "What happens now?"

options.text: "I'll keep you safe, and I'll get us help."
options.then: She squeezes your hand. "You won't leave me?"

options.text: "Nothing. We'll keep this in the family."
options.then: She looks confused. "But he'll still come here."

options.text: "I'm going to go and beat him up."
options.then: She grabs your arm. "No! Please don't!"

options.text: "I'll tell you once I've talked to everyone."
options.then: She looks worried. "Everyone?"

steps.why: A calm promise of safety and help turns her courage into protection.

scenarios.relearn: 'I believe you. It's not your fault. I'll keep you safe.' That response protects a child and aids their recovery.

scenarios.hook: "I should press my child for every detail right away to get the full story."

myth.un: I should press my child for every detail right away to get the full story.
myth.re: Don't interrogate; let the child share at their own pace in their own words, and leave detailed questioning to trained professionals.
myth.why: Listening, not interrogating, is the parent's job.

scenarios.relearn: Don't interrogate a disclosing child; let them share at their own pace, and leave detailed questioning to professionals.

scenarios.hook: Match each disclosure-response step to what it does for the child.

pairs.right: Keeps them talking, not shut down
Lifts the self-blame that silences them

pairs.left: Let the child talk, then act
Get safe help, don't hush it

scenarios.relearn: Assure, believe and stay calm, say it's not their fault, let them talk then act, and get safe help: the steps that protect a disclosing child.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: how you respond in that first moment shapes your child's safety and their healing. Feel the weight?
scenarios.affirm: A parent's response in the first moment of a disclosure profoundly shapes the child's safety and their healing.
scenarios.relearn: How you respond in that first moment shapes your child's safety and their healing.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter Chhaya tells you a relative has been hurting her, and part of you fears a scandal.

steps.prompt: She is watching your face. What do you do first?

options.text: Hold her and say: 'I believe you. It's not your fault'
options.then: Chhaya cries into your shoulder, and her breathing slowly calms.

options.text: Tell her not to repeat this to anyone
options.then: She nods, frightened, and stops talking.

options.text: Ask if she's sure it wasn't a misunderstanding
options.then: She pulls away. 'Forget it. I'm sorry,' she says.

options.text: Say you'll think about what to do, and send her to bed
options.then: She goes, but lies awake wondering if she said something wrong.

steps.why: Belief and no blame come first. They help her feel safe.

steps.prompt: When you tell your mother-in-law, she says reporting it will ruin the family's name. What do you do?

options.text: Say Chhaya's safety matters more than any name
options.then: Your mother-in-law is furious, but you hold firm.

options.text: Agree to handle it quietly within the family
options.then: The relative is warned privately and still comes to family functions.

options.text: Say nothing, and wait for things to calm down
options.then: Days pass. Nothing changes, and the relative still visits.

options.text: Promise to report it only if it happens again
options.then: It feels like a middle path, but Chhaya stays exposed in the meantime.

steps.why: Protecting a child always comes before the family's image.

steps.prompt: That week, the relative is due at your house for a festival. What do you do?

options.text: Keep him away from Chhaya and call Childline 1098
options.then: A counsellor guides you on reporting, and the relative is told not to come.

options.text: Let him come, but keep Chhaya upstairs in her room
options.then: Chhaya spends the festival upstairs, listening to his voice below.

options.text: Let him come and act as if nothing happened
options.then: Chhaya goes silent all evening and won't eat.

options.text: Confront him yourself in front of everyone
options.then: He denies it loudly, and some relatives start doubting Chhaya.

steps.why: Keeping her safe and reaching Childline 1098 puts protection into action.

steps.prompt: Later, Chhaya asks if she has caused trouble for the whole family. What do you tell her?

options.text: No. The one who hurt you caused this, not you
options.then: She lets out a long breath and leans into you.

options.text: It's done now. Let's not talk about it
options.then: She nods, but her eyes stay on the floor.

options.text: A little, but we'll manage somehow
options.then: She starts crying again. 'I'm sorry,' she whispers.

options.text: Don't worry about the family. Just focus on school
options.then: She nods, but still believes she broke something.

steps.why: She needs to hear plainly that the fault is entirely the abuser's, never hers.

scenarios.debrief: After a disclosure, reassure your child, then protect and report, never hushing it up for the family's image.
scenarios.relearn: Protect and report after a disclosure; silencing it for the family's image abandons your child.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: a child has just disclosed. Spot the two responses that harm them.

scene.text: 'I believe you, it's not your fault'
Blaming or doubting them out loud
Staying calm and acting to protect
Interrogating them for every detail
'I'm glad you told me, you're safe now'

scenarios.why: Blame, doubt, and interrogation harm a disclosing child; belief, calm, and 'I'm glad you told me' keep them safe.
scenarios.relearn: Keep a disclosing child safe with belief, 'it's not your fault', and calm protection; blame, doubt, and interrogation harm them.

scenarios.hook: After telling you someone hurt her, your daughter Kavya seems scared of what you now think of her.
scenarios.setup: She follows you into the kitchen.

steps.prompt: Kavya asks: "Do you still love me?"

options.text: "Completely. Nothing changes that."
options.then: She lets out a breath. "Even now?"

options.text: "Why would you even ask me that?"
options.then: She shrugs and looks away.

options.text: "Of course. Now let's talk about something else."
options.then: She nods, but her question hangs there.

options.text: "Yes, but we'll discuss what happened later."
options.then: She stiffens. "Later? What's going to happen?"

steps.why: Unconditional love, said plainly, is what she needs to hear first.

steps.prompt: Kavya asks: "Am I in trouble?"

options.text: "You're not in any trouble. You were so brave."
options.then: Her shoulders drop. "I thought you'd be angry."

options.text: "Not yet, but we'll have to see."
options.then: She goes pale and silent.

options.text: "Only if you hide things from me again."
options.then: She nods quickly. "I won't. I promise."

options.text: "No. Just don't talk about it with anyone."
options.then: She nods. "Not even Nani?"

steps.why: Hearing 'not in trouble' and 'brave' undoes the fear an abuser plants.

steps.prompt: Kavya asks: "Did I do something wrong?"

options.text: "No. It's his fault, not yours. I'll keep you safe."
options.then: She nods slowly. "Okay. I'm glad I told you."

options.text: "You shouldn't have gone over to his house alone."
options.then: Her eyes fill. "I know. I'm sorry."

options.text: "Let's not think about who did what, okay?"
options.then: She frowns. "So maybe I did?"

options.text: "Everyone makes mistakes, beta. It's okay."
options.then: She looks down. "So it was a mistake."

steps.why: The fault is entirely the abuser's, and she needs to hear you'll keep her safe.

scenarios.relearn: Unconditional love, 'not in trouble', 'so brave', 'not your fault' is exactly what a child needs to hear to begin healing.

scenarios.hook: "What counts as abuse is fuzzy, and the child might share the blame."

myth.un: What counts as abuse is fuzzy, and the child might share the blame.
myth.re: Under India's POCSO Act, any sexual offence against anyone under 18 is a crime, and the child is always the victim, never to blame.
myth.why: The law is clear: the child is the protected victim.

scenarios.relearn: Under POCSO, any sexual offence against an under-18 is a crime and the child is always the victim, never to blame.

scenarios.hook: "This is a private family matter; I shouldn't involve the authorities."

myth.un: This is a private family matter; I shouldn't involve the authorities.
myth.re: Child abuse is a crime, not a private matter, and the law obliges reporting; the authorities exist to protect your child.
myth.why: Reporting protects the child and others.

scenarios.relearn: Child abuse is a crime to report, not a private matter; the law obliges it, and reporting protects your child.

scenarios.hook: Match each route to when it's for (India).

pairs.right: Help for a child in danger or distress
Reporting a sexual offence against a child

scenarios.relearn: Childline 1098, police or the e-Box, cybercrime 1930 and 112 are the routes to protect a child.

scenarios.hook: Sort: the right action if a child is being abused, or the wrong one?

items.text: Reporting to Childline or the police
Keeping quiet to avoid scandal
Believing and protecting the child
Confronting the abuser alone, then dropping it

options.text: "We'll believe you. And we'll help, every time."

options.text: "Why wouldn't I? You two never lie to me."

options.text: "I'll believe you, as long as you're telling the truth."
options.then: Isha frowns. "How will you know?"

options.text: "Don't worry about things like that."

steps.prompt: That night, a new message arrives on Dhruv's phone. The person he sent it to wants more. What do you do?

options.text: Keep the chats as evidence and stop replying
options.then: Dhruv saves the username and messages, not the image, and leaves the chat unanswered.

options.text: Ask the person nicely to delete what they have
options.then: They promise to, then ask for money.

options.text: Delete the account and pretend it never happened
options.then: The account is gone, and so is the evidence.

options.text: Message the person yourself and threaten them
options.then: They reply with a threat to share what they have.

steps.why: Evidence and silence stop the pressure and help a report.

steps.prompt: You're unsure whether to get outside help. What do you do?

options.text: Report it to cybercrime 1930
options.then: The helpline takes the details and explains how they can help.

options.text: Handle it quietly within the family
options.then: Days pass, and Dhruv checks his phone every few minutes, frightened.

options.text: Ask Dhruv's school friends what they know
options.then: Soon half his class is talking about it.

options.text: Wait to see if the person goes quiet
options.then: The person goes quiet for a week, then messages again.

steps.why: Getting help through cybercrime 1930 turns fear into a handled situation.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, Dhruv says he still feels stupid. What do you tell him?

options.text: You were tricked. That's on them, not you
options.then: He nods slowly. 'I just wish I'd told you sooner.'

options.text: Well, lesson learned, I hope
options.then: He winces and goes back to his room.

options.text: Let's never talk about it again
options.then: He nods, and carries the shame alone.

options.text: Everyone makes mistakes online at your age
options.then: He shrugs, still thinking it was mostly his fault.

steps.why: A teenager pressured online is a victim, never at fault.

scenarios.debrief: If a child regrets something shared online, reassure them, keep evidence and get help, never shaming them.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Ritu calls, panicking. A stranger has been sending her son Samar frightening messages online.
scenarios.setup: You can hear her pacing as she talks.

steps.prompt: Ritu says: "I'm going to smash his phone. I can't think straight."

options.text: "Wait. Take a breath. The phone has the proof you'll need."
options.then: Ritu stops pacing. "Proof. Okay. What do I do with it?"

options.text: "Honestly, smashing it sounds fair after all this."
options.then: "Right," Ritu says. "I'll smash it once I've seen to Samar."

options.text: "How did Samar even let a stranger talk to him?"
options.then: Ritu's voice cracks. "So this is his fault too?"

options.text: "Calm down. It's probably just some kid messing about."
options.then: Ritu goes quiet. "You didn't see the messages."

steps.why: Steadying her first stops the panic from destroying the evidence.

steps.prompt: Ritu asks: "Samar is crying in his room. What do I even say to him?"

options.text: "Tell him he's off the internet until he learns."
options.then: Ritu hesitates. "He'll think he's being punished."

options.text: "Tell him it's not his fault, and you're glad he told you."
options.then: "Not his fault," she repeats. "Yes. He needs to hear that."

options.text: "Leave him alone for now. He'll come round on his own by morning."
options.then: "Okay," Ritu says, unsure. "I'll give him space."

options.text: "Ask him exactly what he said to the stranger."
options.then: "He'll clam up," Ritu says. "He always does when I push."

steps.why: A child targeted online needs to hear he's not to blame.

steps.prompt: Ritu says: "My husband thinks we should just keep this quiet."

options.text: "Quiet only helps the stranger. Report it to cybercrime 1930."
options.then: Ritu writes the number down. "Okay. I'll tell him that."

options.text: "He might be right. Why make it into a big deal?"
options.then: Ritu sighs. "So we just hope it stops?"

options.text: "Post a warning in your building's WhatsApp group."
options.then: "Everyone will know it was Samar," Ritu says, alarmed.

options.text: "Tell Samar's school, and let the teachers sort it out for you."
options.then: "The school can't stop a stranger online," Ritu says slowly.

steps.why: Reporting to 1930 is how online targeting gets stopped. Silence doesn't stop it.

steps.prompt: Ritu asks: "What if the stranger messages again tonight?"

options.text: "Reply and say you're the police. That'll scare him."
options.then: Ritu hesitates. "What if it makes him angrier?"

options.text: "Block him on everything straight away, then delete."
options.then: "Yes," Ritu says. "Then I'll never have to see it again."

options.text: "Stay up and watch Samar's phone all night."
options.then: "All night?" Ritu asks. "I'm already exhausted."

options.text: "Don't reply. Screenshot it, and keep it as proof."
options.then: "No reply. Just screenshots," she says. "I can do that."

steps.why: Every new message is more proof for a report, so save it and don't engage.

scenarios.relearn: Steadying a friend toward reassurance, evidence and reporting protects the child better than a panicked over-reaction.

steps.prompt: Pallavi asks: "Why now? Nothing's happened to our kids."

options.text: "That's why. Let's save Childline 1098 and 1930 now."

options.text: "You're right. We'll look them up if we ever need them."
options.then: She nods and goes back to her bills.

options.text: "Because the world is full of predators now."
options.then: Pallavi looks up from the screen. "Don't scare me like that."

options.text: "Just in case. I'll save them on my own phone for us."
options.then: "Okay," she says. "You're the organised one."

steps.prompt: Later, Pallavi asks: "Which number would even be for what?"

options.text: "1098 if a child is hurt, 1930 online, 112 in danger."
options.then: She types them in, saying each one out loud.

options.text: "Just call the police for anything. It's simpler."
options.then: She saves just the police number. "One is easier to remember."

options.text: "I'm not sure. We'll work it out on the day."
options.then: She shrugs, and saves them with no idea which is which.

options.text: "Any of them. They all do the same thing, really."
options.then: "Do they?" she asks, doubtful.

steps.prompt: Pallavi asks: "Should we tell the kids about these numbers too?"

options.text: "Yes, and that they can always come to us first."

options.text: "No. It'll only frighten them for no reason."

options.text: "Yes. Then they won't need to come to us with it."

options.text: "Let's wait until they're teenagers for that."
options.then: "That's years away," she says.

steps.why: Children stay safer when they know the numbers and that your door is always open.

scenarios.relearn: Saving the key helplines in advance means that in a frightening moment, the right help is instantly to hand.

scenarios.hook: Months after your son Babu told you what happened and you reported it, he seems more like himself.
scenarios.setup: Tonight he's helping you roll rotis.

steps.prompt: Babu asks quietly: "Are you still sad about what happened?"

options.text: "I'm proud of you. You were so brave to tell me."
options.then: Babu smiles shyly. "I was really scared."

options.text: "Let's never mention it again. It's embarrassing."
options.then: Babu's smile fades. He rolls the next roti in silence.

options.text: "I'm fine. Don't you worry about me."
options.then: Babu nods, but keeps watching your face.

options.text: "Yes. I wish it had never happened to our family."
options.then: Babu looks down. "Sorry, Amma."

steps.why: Naming his bravery helps him see telling you as strength, not trouble.

steps.prompt: Babu says: "Sometimes I think it happened because I was bad."

options.text: "None of it was your fault. Not one bit."
options.then: Babu's eyes fill up. "Promise?"

options.text: "You weren't bad. But you must be more careful now."
options.then: "Careful how?" he asks, worried.

options.text: "Don't think about it. Think about school."
options.then: "Okay," he says, and goes quiet.

options.text: "Why would you think that? That's silly."
options.then: Babu shrugs and looks away.

steps.why: Hearing clearly that it wasn't his fault helps him heal. The blame is the abuser's alone.

steps.prompt: Babu asks: "What if something bad happens again?"

options.text: "Then tell me, anytime. I'll always listen and help."
options.then: He leans against you. "Anytime?"

options.text: "It won't. I'll never let you out of my sight again."
options.then: Babu looks alarmed. "Never?"

options.text: "Then you'll know better and handle it yourself."
options.then: Babu frowns. "By myself?"

options.text: "Let's not talk about bad things before bed."
options.then: He nods and says nothing more.

steps.why: A permanent open door tells him he'll never face anything alone.

scenarios.relearn: Affirming a child's bravery, their blamelessness and your permanent open door supports healing far more than silence.

scenarios.source: even if they said not to
scenarios.hook: Bedtime is calm, and you want to plant the open-door message with your daughter Lakshmi.
scenarios.setup: She's tucked in, holding your hand.

steps.prompt: Lakshmi asks: "Amma, will you tell me a story?"

options.text: "First, listen. If anyone scares or confuses you, always tell me."
options.then: "Always?" she asks, sleepy. "Even at night?"

options.text: "Not tonight. Just be a good girl and sleep."
options.then: She turns over, then turns back. "Amma, can I ask you something?"

options.text: "Only if you promise to stay out of trouble."
options.then: "I promise," she says, unsure what trouble means. Then she frowns, thinking.

options.text: "Yes, and then be extra good tomorrow, okay?"
options.then: She smiles. "I'm always good." Then her smile fades. "Amma?"

steps.why: Saying it plainly at a calm moment makes the message stick.

steps.prompt: Lakshmi whispers: "Amma, what if someone tells me a secret and says not to tell you?"

options.text: "Tell me anyway. Even at midnight."
options.then: She thinks. "Even if it's someone big?"

options.text: "Then listen to them if they're a grown-up."
options.then: "Okay," she says. "Grown-ups know best."

options.text: "Nobody will ever say that to you."
options.then: "But what if they do?" she asks again.

options.text: "Tell me only if it's something really, really bad."
options.then: She frowns. "How bad is really bad?"

steps.why: Telling her ahead to come even if someone said not to breaks the secrecy abusers rely on.

steps.prompt: Lakshmi asks: "And what if it's someone we love?"

options.text: "Even then. You'll never be in trouble for telling."
options.then: She squeezes your hand. "Okay, Amma."

options.text: "People who love us would never hurt us."
options.then: She nods, reassured. "So only strangers are the bad ones."

options.text: "Let's not talk about scary things at bedtime."
options.then: She goes quiet and pulls the sheet over her head.

options.text: "Yes, but only if you're really sure that it's wrong."
options.then: "How will I know if I'm sure?" she whispers.

steps.why: Most harm comes from someone known, so she needs to know no one outranks telling you.

scenarios.relearn: Telling a child in advance to come to you even if someone said not to dismantles the secrecy abusers rely on.

scenarios.hook: Your son Om starts to tell you a worry about his tuition class, then stops halfway.
scenarios.setup: He's fiddling with his bag strap, eyes down.

steps.prompt: Om mumbles: "Never mind. Forget it."

options.text: "It's okay. Take your time. I'm right here."
options.then: He glances up. "It's kind of weird to say."

options.text: "Fine. Don't waste my time then."
options.then: He shrugs and walks off to his room.

options.text: "No, you started it. Now finish it."
options.then: He shakes his head. "It's nothing. Really."

options.text: "Okay. If it's nothing, then it's nothing."
options.then: He looks relieved, and the moment passes.

steps.why: Patient warmth keeps the door open for the rest.

steps.prompt: Later that evening, Om says: "You'll think I'm being silly."

options.text: "I won't. Whatever it is, I want to hear it."
options.then: He sits down. "The tuition sir keeps making me stay back alone."

options.text: "You probably are, but go on then."
options.then: Om's face closes. "See? Never mind."

options.text: "Everyone worries about silly things. It's normal."
options.then: He shrugs. "Yeah. It's probably nothing."

options.text: "Then don't bother telling me at all."
options.then: He goes quiet and turns on the TV.

steps.why: Promising to take it seriously helps him risk saying it.

steps.prompt: At bedtime, Om asks: "If I tell you the rest, will you make a big fuss?"

options.text: "I'll stay calm, and I'll help. Telling me is right."
options.then: He nods slowly, then tells you the rest, watching your face.

options.text: "Okay. I won't do anything at all."
options.then: He relaxes. "Good. Just forget I said it."

options.text: "Of course I will. This is serious!"
options.then: He shrinks back. "I knew I shouldn't have said."

options.text: "Fine, but you're never going to tuition again."
options.then: "What? Everyone will ask why!" he says, upset.

steps.why: Being calm and honest about helping, without promising to do nothing, keeps him safe and trusting.

scenarios.relearn: When a child half-tells then retreats, a patient 'Take your time. I'm here.' keeps the door open for the rest.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter Fatima admits she broke the expensive mixer grinder and was terrified to say so.
scenarios.setup: She's holding out the cracked jar with both hands.

steps.prompt: Fatima says: "I'm sorry. I was scared you'd be so angry."

options.text: "Thank you for telling me. That was brave."
options.then: She blinks. "You're not angry?"

options.text: "Do you know how much that cost us?"
options.then: She starts crying. "I'm sorry. I'm sorry."

options.text: "Next time, just be more careful, okay?"
options.then: "Okay," she whispers, still waiting for the shouting.

options.text: "Go to your room. I'll deal with you later."
options.then: She runs to her room, then creeps back to the doorway, eyes red.

steps.why: Thanking her first teaches that telling you is always the safe choice.

steps.prompt: Fatima asks: "Will you tell Abbu?"

options.text: "Yes, and I'll tell him how brave you were."
options.then: She smiles a little. "Okay. Will he be angry?"

options.text: "No. This stays our little secret."
options.then: She looks relieved. "Good. Don't tell anyone."

options.text: "Yes, and he can decide your punishment."
options.then: She goes pale. "Please don't."

options.text: "Maybe. It depends on how you behave."
options.then: She nods, anxious, and watches you all afternoon.

steps.why: Being open about what happens next, and praising her, keeps her trust whole.

steps.prompt: That night, Fatima asks: "Do you still love me even though I broke it?"

options.text: "Always. Things can be fixed. You matter more."
options.then: She hugs you tight. "I love you too, Ammi."

options.text: "Of course, but I'm very disappointed."
options.then: She nods and lets go of your hand.

options.text: "Don't be dramatic. It's only a mixer."
options.then: She looks embarrassed. "Sorry. Goodnight."

options.text: "Yes, as long as it doesn't happen again."
options.then: Her smile falters. "Okay. I'll be careful."

steps.why: Putting her above the broken thing teaches that telling you never costs her your love.

scenarios.relearn: Thanking a child for a hard admission, over the broken thing, teaches that telling you is always the safe choice.

scenarios.hook: Your son Sonu says his uncle's tickling 'games' make him uncomfortable.

options.text: "Did you do something to start the game?"

options.text: "I won't ever let him find out that you told me."

scenarios.relearn: Believing a child's discomfort with a relative, and acting on it, teaches that their 'no' is always heard at home.

scenarios.hook: While you're cooking, your son Kunal, 7, comes to you with a frank question about his body.

options.text: "Go and ask your father about that one."

options.text: "Just call it your 'down there' for now."
options.then: He nods. "Down there. Okay."

options.text: "Rohan's word is fine. Everyone uses it."

steps.prompt: Kunal asks: "Can I ask you anything about my body?"

scenarios.relearn: Answer body questions calmly and say you're glad they asked, so a child keeps coming to you, not strangers.

scenarios.hook: Your son Aarav confesses he lied today about being at a friend's house. He was at the gaming parlour.

options.text: "It took courage to tell me. Let's talk about it."

options.text: "Liar. I won't believe a single word you say now."
options.then: His eyes fill. "Then why did I even tell you?"

options.text: "Yes. No going out for a whole month."
options.then: He nods stiffly. "Okay. Got it."

options.text: "Forget it. Just don't ever do it again."
options.then: "Okay," he says, surprised, but he lingers by the door.

steps.why: Valuing the confession keeps him choosing honesty with you.

steps.prompt: Aarav asks: "Why does it even matter where I was?"

options.text: "So I know where to find you if something goes wrong."
options.then: He thinks about it. "Okay. That makes sense."

options.text: "Because gaming parlours are full of bad people."

steps.prompt: Aarav asks: "So what do I do next time I want to go to the parlour?"

options.text: "Tell me only if it's somewhere I'd approve of."
options.then: He looks away. "So I just won't mention the parlour."

options.text: "We'll see. You have to earn my trust back first."

options.text: "Just ask your mother. She handles all this."
options.then: "Okay," he says, and the moment with you passes.

scenarios.relearn: Valuing the truth-telling over the lie keeps a child choosing honesty with you, even when it's hard.

scenarios.hook: Your autistic son Dev comes home from school upset, struggling to find any words.
scenarios.setup: He's sitting on the floor, hands over his ears.

steps.prompt: Dev says: "Can't. Can't say it."

options.text: "That's okay. Show me, draw it, or write it."
options.then: He looks at his notebook. "Draw?"

options.text: "Use your words properly, or I can't help you."
options.then: He rocks harder. "Can't. Can't."

options.text: "Stop being difficult and just tell me."
options.then: He turns away and hums loudly.

options.text: "Okay. We'll talk about it tomorrow instead."
options.then: He nods, still rocking. "Tomorrow."

steps.why: Offering other ways to tell makes telling possible for him.

steps.prompt: Dev says: "Too loud. Everything too loud."

options.text: "Let's go somewhere quiet first. No rush."
options.then: He follows you to his room and breathes more slowly. "Quiet."

options.text: "It's not loud here. You're overreacting."
options.then: He covers his ears tighter. "Loud."

options.text: "Tell me quickly and then it'll be over."
options.then: He shakes his head hard. "No."

options.text: "Here, watch your cartoon and forget about it."
options.then: He calms with the cartoon. "Forget," he repeats.

steps.why: Calm and quiet come first. A settled child can tell you more.

steps.prompt: Dev hands you a drawing and says: "Bus. Big boy."

options.text: "Thank you for showing me. Take your time."
options.then: He taps the drawing. "Takes my bag. Every day."

options.text: "Which big boy? What's his name? When was it?"

options.text: "Big boys are just playing. Ignore them."
options.then: He takes the drawing back. "Not playing."

options.text: "Okay, I'm calling the school right now."
options.then: He grabs your arm. "No! Not finished!"

steps.why: Thanks and patience let him finish telling you in his own way.

scenarios.relearn: Letting a child tell their own way, with words, drawing or showing, makes you tellable for a child who finds speech hard.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter Pooja hesitantly says her older cousin asked her to keep a 'secret game' between them.
scenarios.setup: She's whispering, even though you're alone.

steps.prompt: Pooja asks: "Am I bad for telling you? I promised."

options.text: "No. Uneasy secrets are the ones to bring me."
options.then: She nods slowly. "It did feel weird."

options.text: "If you promised, you should keep your word."
options.then: She looks at her feet. "Okay. Sorry."

options.text: "What game? What did he make you do?"
options.then: She freezes. "Nothing. I don't know."

options.text: "Don't worry. Cousins play silly games all the time."
options.then: She shrugs. "Okay," she says, but doesn't look sure.

steps.why: Praising her for breaking an uneasy secret teaches that no one outranks telling you.

steps.prompt: Pooja says: "He said I'd get in trouble if anyone knew."

options.text: "You're not in trouble. You did right."

options.text: "He was probably just teasing you, beta."

options.text: "I won't tell anyone, so you're safe."
options.then: She relaxes. "Promise? Not even Papa?"

steps.prompt: Pooja asks: "What will happen now?"

options.text: "I'm going to go and shout at him right now."

options.text: "You'll just stay away from him from now on."
options.then: She nods. "But he's at every family function."

steps.why: A calm plan with an adult in charge shows her telling you leads to safety.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Pooja asks: "Can I still play with my other cousins?"

options.text: "Of course. Telling me doesn't take anything away."

options.text: "Maybe not for a while, just to be safe."
options.then: Her face falls. "Because I told?"

options.text: "Only if you don't tell anyone else about any of this."
options.then: She nods, confused. "Okay. I won't."

steps.why: Keeping her life normal shows her that telling never costs her anything.

scenarios.relearn: Praising a child for breaking an uneasy 'secret' teaches that no one, not even a cousin, outranks telling you.

scenarios.hook: Earlier, you snapped at your son Yash when he tried to tell you something, and it's bothering you.

options.text: "I'm sorry I got short with you earlier."

options.text: "What's done is done. Goodnight, beta."

options.text: "You know I was tired. Don't sulk about it."
options.then: He turns a page. "I'm not sulking."

options.text: "Shall we get ice cream tomorrow, just us two?"
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay," he says, eyes still on the book.

steps.prompt: Yash asks: "So was I wrong to tell you?"

options.text: "No. You did nothing wrong. Always come to me."

options.text: "It was just bad timing on your part. That's all."
options.then: He frowns. "So I should wait till you're happy?"

options.text: "Let's not go over it all again tonight."
options.then: He shrugs. "Okay." He goes back to reading.

options.text: "That depends on what it was about."
options.then: His face closes. "Forget it then."

steps.why: Telling him the telling wasn't the problem restores his trust to try again.

options.text: "Thank you for telling me. I'm listening."

options.then: Yash hesitates. "I don't remember exactly."

options.text: "Drivers joke around. I'm sure it's nothing."

options.text: "Right. I'm calling the school this minute."
options.then: Yash panics. "Wait! I haven't finished!"

options.text: "Let's keep this between us for now, okay?"

scenarios.relearn: A calm repair after snapping, saying sorry and that they did nothing wrong by telling you, restores a child's trust to tell again.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter Pinky says she feels awkward when her tuition teacher hugs her for too long.

options.then: She thinks. "What if he doesn't let me?"

options.text: "Fine. I won't say anything to anyone."
options.then: She relaxes. "Thank you, Amma. Our secret."

options.then: Pinky's eyes widen. "No! He'll be angry with me!"

options.text: "Thanks for telling me. I'll talk to the centre head."

options.text: "Just stay away from all the male teachers."

scenarios.relearn: Backing a child's 'this felt wrong' about any adult, and acting, proves telling you is always worth it.

options.then: He nods. "Okay. I'll remember."

scenarios.hook: "If what my child describes sounds far-fetched, it probably didn't really happen."

myth.re: Children very rarely invent abuse; a confusing or partial account is normal, so believe them and let the details come later.

scenarios.relearn: A child's account can sound confused or incomplete and still be true; believe them, and don't treat oddness as proof they made it up.

scenarios.hook: "My child told me weeks after it happened, so they're probably exaggerating now."

myth.un: My child told me weeks after it happened, so they're probably exaggerating now.
myth.re: Delay is one of the most normal things about disclosure; fear and confusion keep children silent, and a late telling is just as real.
myth.why: A delay is fear, not a lie.

scenarios.relearn: Children often disclose long after harm; treat a delayed telling as real and brave, never as a sign they are exaggerating.

scenarios.hook: "If I stay calm while my child tells me something awful, they'll think I don't care."

myth.un: If I stay calm while my child tells me something awful, they'll think I don't care.
myth.re: Your calm tells a child it is safe to keep talking; a steady, warm face reassures far more than visible shock or rage.
myth.why: Calm reads as safety, not as not caring.

scenarios.relearn: Staying calm during a disclosure is an act of care, not coldness; it keeps a child talking instead of frightening them into silence.

scenarios.hook: "When my child discloses, I should march straight to confront the person they named."

scenarios.hook: "My child seemed calm telling me, so it can't have been serious."

myth.un: My child seemed calm telling me, so it can't have been serious.
myth.re: Children disclose in all kinds of ways, sometimes flatly or matter-of-factly; a calm telling can carry the most serious news.
myth.why: How they tell you isn't how big it is.

scenarios.relearn: A child may disclose serious harm calmly or flatly; never measure how serious it is by how upset they seem while telling you.

scenarios.hook: "If my child says they're partly to blame, I should agree so they learn to be careful."

myth.un: If my child says they're partly to blame, I should agree so they learn to be careful.
myth.re: A child is never to blame for abuse; when they blame themselves, your job is to say clearly that the fault is entirely the adult's.

scenarios.hook: Your daughter Seema whispers that her uncle has been touching her.

options.text: "I'm not angry with you. I'm glad you told me."
options.then: She lets out a breath. "I was so scared to say."

options.then: Seema flinches and starts to cry. "I'm sorry!"

options.text: "I'm not angry. Just tell me everything, slowly."
options.then: She tries, then stops. "I don't want to say it."

options.text: "Of course, but why didn't you tell me sooner?"
options.then: She shrinks. "I didn't know how."

options.text: "Let's not talk about that part right now."
options.then: She stares at you. "So you don't?"

steps.why: Believing her fully, and saying it's not her fault, is vital to her safety and recovery.

steps.prompt: Seema asks: "Will I have to see Mama again?"

options.text: "No. I'll keep you away from him and get us help."
options.then: She hugs you tight. "Thank you, Amma."

options.text: "He's family. We can't avoid him forever."
options.then: She goes very still. "Okay," she whispers.

options.text: "Only at big family functions, and I'll stay close."
options.then: She nods, but her hands are shaking. "Okay."

options.text: "We'll decide that later, with everyone."
options.then: She looks panicked. "Everyone will know?"

steps.why: Keeping her away from him and getting help puts her safety first.

steps.prompt: That night, Seema asks: "Can I sleep next to you?"

options.text: "Yes. You're safe with me."
options.then: She curls up close. "Okay, Amma."

options.text: "You're a big girl. Sleep in your own bed."
options.then: She goes, but leaves the light on. "Goodnight."

options.text: "Yes, if you tell me everything that happened."
options.then: She turns away. "I don't want to."

options.text: "Yes, but don't tell Papa about any of this."
options.then: She nods, frightened. "It's a secret?"

scenarios.relearn: 'I'm not angry with you. I believe you. It's not your fault. I'm glad you told me.' This keeps a child safe and talking.
